entry.title: Subnetting and CIDR Notation: A Practical Guide
entry.summary:
Working out whether 192.168.1.130 is on the same network as 192.168.1.73/26 should take a few seconds. Guess wrong and you end up with a VPN range that swallows your LAN, or a firewall rule that matches far more than you meant. This guide shows how CIDR notation maps to bits, how to find network and broadcast addresses by hand, how to carve a /24 into subnets for a home lab, and how to check what your Linux hosts are configured with. An IPv4 address is a 32-bit number. Dotted-quad notation splits it into four 8-bit octets and writes each one in decimal, so every octet runs from 0 to 255. 192 .168 .1 .73 11000000 10101000 00000001 01001001

entry.title: The Agent Added a Second Copy of a Utility the Repo Already Had
entry.summary: Quick answer: When an agent adds a "small helper" that already exists elsewhere in the repo, you don't just have a duplicate file. You now have two functions that look identical today but will drift apart the first time someone fixes a bug in one of them. Treat the discovery of an existing utility as a hard stop: reuse it, or deliberately consolidate, never silently fork it. I found the pattern on a routine review of a checkout change. The agent had introduced formatMoneyCents() in a new pricing.ts. It was well written, it had a unit test, and the feature worked. entry.title: The eMudhra fix lives in your Go binary, not in your Docker image
entry.summary: On October 19, Go shipped two security releases: 1.27.3 and 1.26.10. The fix touches a single package, crypto/x509. I rebuilt one of my Go services on the same Docker image as before. Go's own scanner still found the flaw. TL;DR: the eMudhra fix is a list of eight banned keys, written into the code of crypto/x509. That list is compiled into your binary. Updating the base image or the system certificates does not add it. You have to rebuild with Go 1.27.3 or 1.26.10, then redeploy. If your Dockerfile still builds with Go 1.25, rebuilding changes nothing: that version gets no more fixes. Versions and source status: snapshot as of October 31, 2026. entry.title: Linux SysAdmin Interview Questions 2021 Part 2
entry.summary:
Q9. A user sees “This account is currently not available” at a terminal, or the GUI returns to the login prompt. How do you troubleshoot it?
Start by inspecting the account rather than editing /etc/passwd directly: getent passwd nerds
The final field is the user's login shell. If it is /sbin/nologin or /usr/sbin/nologin, an interactive login normally prints a “not available” message. If it is /bin/false, the shell exits immediately and may simply return to a login prompt. These are not necessarily errors: service accounts are often deliberately prevented from logging in interactively. For a real user account that should have terminal access, change the shell with usermod: sudo usermod -s /bin/bash nerds getent passwd nerds
You can also use chsh -s /bin/bash nerds where permitted. Avoid…
